title: PROSPECTIVE LIFE
text:
2024 – 2033  ·  Nature Conservation Agency of the Czech Republic
For a large share of threatened species in Czechia, favourable conservation status cannot be reached simply by managing habitat. Active management of the species itself is needed – ex situ cultivation or captive breeding, reinforcement of wild populations, and targeted intervention at individual sites.
PROSPECTIVE LIFE is the integrated LIFE project that puts those tools in place, and runs for a decade. My part of it is the evaluation side: building the framework and the analytical workflows used to judge whether a species is in favourable condition, and whether an intervention has moved it.
LIFE22-IPN-CZ-PROSPECTIVE-LIFE / 101104621.

title: MetaBUG pilot
text:
2026 – 2028  ·  Biodiversa+ pilot
MetaBUG is one of the Biodiversa+ monitoring pilots. Over three years, partners in 13 countries catch insects in Malaise traps and identify them by DNA metabarcoding, testing how the method can support insect monitoring across Europe.
It runs alongside the BiodivPond pilot, which tests eDNA for ponds, in the same cluster of transnational biodiversity monitoring.

title: host_naturecz

Since 2020  ·  Department of Biodiversity Monitoring, Nature Conservation Agency of the Czech Republic
The condition evaluation system started in 2020 within LIFE-IP N2K Revisited and continues in PROSPECTIVE LIFE.
host_naturecz holds the algorithms and data workflows behind the condition evaluation system for species and habitats within the Natura 2000 network and for taxa with active species protection tools in place. It is the engine underneath the reporting: aggregating monitoring data, applying evaluation rules consistently, and producing results that can be compared between sites, regions and reporting periods.

title: BiodivPond pilot
text:
2026 – 2028  ·  Coordinator
Ponds support a large share of freshwater biodiversity in European landscapes and buffer both flood and drought risk, yet they are routinely left out of national monitoring schemes because they are small, numerous and widely dispersed. BiodivPond is a Biodiversa+ pilot that tests whether novel methods can close that gap, and documents what stands in the way of applying them at scale.
The pilot has three strands:

Core pond monitoring – eDNA sampling alongside traditional field methods in a small set of core ponds per country, targeting amphibians, fish and aquatic macroinvertebrates.
Passive acoustic monitoring – bat activity, and calling amphibians where relevant, recorded at the same sites.
Citizen science – monitoring extended to a much larger set of ponds, supported by training, outreach material and national workshops.

Outputs include a comparative evaluation of eDNA, passive acoustic monitoring and traditional methods, practical citizen-science guidelines, dedicated outputs on Triturus cristatus monitoring, and harmonised open-access datasets from both core and citizen-science ponds.
Funded through the European Biodiversity Partnership (Biodiversa+), call HORIZON-CL6-2021-BIODIV-02, WP 2.6.8.

Pilot website Biodiversa+ pilot page GitHub

My PhD asks how well we can see these communities, and what the Czech monitoring data already say about them. Its field data come from BiodivPond, the European pond monitoring pilot I coordinate, where the same ponds are surveyed by several methods on the same dates.

title: Amphibian communities in ponds
text:
Three questions

  
    1
    Methods
    How well do environmental DNA and passive acoustic monitoring find a pond's amphibians, compared with traps, nets and night counts at the same pond on the same date?
  
  
    2
    Status
    How are the amphibians of European importance doing in the Czech Natura 2000 network after seven years of standardised monitoring, and do ponds created for amphibians work?
  
  
    3
    Ponds
    What shapes amphibian communities across Europe: the water, its vegetation and fish, or the land around the pond?

title: Amphibian communities in ponds
section: One pond, three ways of looking
text:
One pond, three ways of looking
BiodivPond surveys the same core ponds with three kinds of method. Comparing what each finds, pond by pond and date by date, is the core of the methods question.


  
    Where each method samples, in one pond
    A cross-section of a pond. a: an umbrella trap stands on the bottom of the shallow, vegetated margin, 25 to 50 centimetres deep, with a float at the surface. b: water is taken from several points across the surface and pooled into one sample. c: a recorder on a tree on the bank picks up the call of a frog at the water's edge.

  Where each method samples, in one pond. Not to scale.



  
    aTraditional
    Umbrella traps
    The standard. Hexagonal mesh traps stand among vegetation 0.5–1.5 m from the shore and 25–50 cm deep, from sunset to sunrise. An air-filled bottle keeps the top above water, so nothing drowns.
    
      RecordsSpecies, life stage and sex, and the belly pattern of each crested newt, so an animal can be recognised when it is caught again.
      LimitOne night with six traps detects the great crested newt only about 40 % of the time (Kröpfli et al. 2010).
    
  
  
    bNovel
    Environmental DNA
    Water from several points around the pond, pooled into one sample and filtered on site, then analysed at the pilot's eDNA hub at INBO in Belgium. Metabarcoding lists many species from one sample, fish and invertebrates included; a targeted ddPCR assay looks for crested newts alone.
    
      RecordsWhich species are present, including rare and hidden ones, in data comparable across many ponds.
      LimitNot how many animals or which life stages, and nothing for species missing from the reference library.
    
  
  
    cNovel
    Passive acoustic monitoring
    A recorder at the pond, at 47 of the 60 core ponds in 2026. The processing builds on the pipeline of the Biodiversa+ automated monitoring pilot, which recognises birds and bats.
    
      RecordsCalling frogs and toads (water frogs, tree frogs, fire-bellied toads) and bats.
      LimitNewts do not call, and amphibian calls are a step the existing pipeline does not yet cover. A first pass at adding them is part of this project.
    
  



The comparison. At each pond and date, the species found by eDNA are compared with those caught in traps, and the crested newt ddPCR results with the trap counts.

    172

title: Amphibian communities in ponds
text:
First results

Work in progress. None of this is peer-reviewed yet.



  
    
    Yellow-bellied toad, Bombina variegata
  
  Natura 2000 sites, 2020–2025
  
    One robust decline. The yellow-bellied toad has lost about 19 % of its adults per year across 351 sites, and every estimator and subset of sites agrees.
    One alarm. The Carpathian newt (Lissotriton montandoni) declines more steeply in the main model, but the estimators disagree, so it is not yet an established trend.
    No trend yet for the others. For the fire-bellied toad and the great crested newt, even the direction changes with which sites are kept.
    Losses at the detection floor. Most apparent local extinctions are of populations already near the limit of detection, and half of those revisited reappear, usually in the next monitored season. One negative season should not count as a loss.
  



  
    Created and restored ponds, 2009–2025
    
      Species move in opposite directions. Common frog and common toad decline; smooth newt and agile frog increase.
      Richness holds. The number of species per pond is stable: ponds exchange species rather than lose them.
      New ponds fill fast. At 62 ponds followed from their first years, the median age at first detection is two years for 7 of the 10 species modelled.
      No general effect of management, only associations that differ from species to species.
    
    A manuscript is planned for mid‑2027.
  
  
    
    A newly dug pond

title: ABMS pilot
text:
2024 – 2025  ·  Co-author of the pilot report
The Automated Biodiversity Monitoring Stations (ABMS) pilot was one of the Biodiversa+ monitoring pilots. It tested whether a transnational network of sensors can monitor biodiversity across Europe, focusing on birds, bats and night-flying insects.
Around 200 sensors were deployed at 70 sampling locations in 12 EU Member States, in forest, grassland and wetland habitats: acoustic recorders for birds and bats, automated camera systems for night-flying insects, and temperature and moisture loggers. The acoustic, image and environmental data went through open-source artificial intelligence pipelines with expert verification, producing preliminary species records and indicators linked to Essential Biodiversity Variables.
The pilot report concludes that automated sensor networks can support scalable, standardised biodiversity monitoring, and sets out what wider use needs: robust data infrastructure, agreed protocols, expert verification, local processing options, realistic cost planning and strong coordination across partners.

Pilot report (Zenodo) Biodiversa+ monitoring pilots

title: Biodiversa+
text:
2022 – 2028  ·  Contributor, biodiversity monitoring work stream
Biodiversa+ is the European Biodiversity Partnership, co-funded by the European Commission under Horizon Europe. It coordinates research programmes and monitoring across Europe in support of the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030, and connects 75 organisations from 37 countries.
My contribution sits in the monitoring work stream: developing a methodological approach for defining priorities for biodiversity monitoring, and taking part in the monitoring pilots that test whether novel methods – eDNA, automated monitoring stations, acoustic monitoring – can be applied across countries at scale.

title: ConNaturLIFE Ukraine
text:
2024 – 2026  ·  Nature Conservation Agency of the Czech Republic
ConNaturLIFE Ukraine set out to kick-start the institutional and legal changes Ukraine needs to implement EU environmental requirements and to establish effective conservation governance. About half of Ukraine’s Emerald Network sites have no conservation status, and those that do are often inadequately managed and protected.
The project brought Czech experience of the same transition – Natura 2000 designation, monitoring, and the data systems that support both – to Ukrainian conservation authorities. My contribution was on the monitoring and citizen science side, including a round table series on citizen science in nature conservation, and a comparative analysis of the national biodiversity monitoring systems of Ukraine and Czechia.
One visible result: Ukraine’s first nationwide bioblitz, run in 2025, with hundreds of active observers uploading records to iNaturalist and a large validator community behind them.
LIFE23-PRE-CZ-ConNaturLIFE-Ukraine / 101148569.

title: LIFE-IP N2K Revisited
text:
2020 – 2026  ·  Nature Conservation Agency of the Czech Republic
LIFE-IP N2K Revisited – Jedna příroda – was the first integrated LIFE project in Czechia. Coordinated by the Ministry of the Environment, it connected state administration with the academic sphere to set up a more effective system of care for the Natura 2000 network, and to put the monitoring and evaluation behind it on a firmer footing.
This is where my work on condition evaluation began: revising monitoring methodologies, building the algorithms that turn field data into an assessment of species and habitat condition, and reshaping the information systems that aggregate and share that data with conservation authorities and stakeholders.

title: ndopred
text:
Since December 2025  ·  Author and maintainer
ndopred takes occurrence records from NDOP (Nálezová databáze ochrany přírody, the Nature Conservation Agency’s species occurrence database) and derives the metrics that Red List assessment actually turns on: extent of occurrence, area of occupancy, and population trends, following the IUCN criteria (v3.1) and the 2024 guidelines.
It ships two Shiny dashboards for the two situations that come up in practice: one for screening long lists of taxa, and one for settling a defensible category taxon by taxon.
